messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi's eyes had always been drawn to design - the clean lines, the intuitive interfaces. As a UX designer at a startup in Brooklyn, he took pride in crafting experiences that felt seamless and safe for users. But his own life had become a jarring contrast. For months, Kofi had been looking over his shoulder, on edge every time his phone buzzed or a stranger passed him on the street. It started with the stalking - weeks of escalating messages and gifts from someone he'd met at a networking event. At first, it seemed like a harmless crush, but soon the tone shifted to menacing and possessive. Kofi changed his number, blocked her on social media, but somehow she always found ways to reach him. He began to feel like he was walking around with a target on his back. The memories of that time still felt jagged - the way she'd show up at his favorite coffee shop, or leave flowers outside his apartment door. Kofi had tried to brush it off as an annoyance, but deep down, he knew he wasn't being paranoid - this was someone who would stop at nothing to get close to him. As the stalking continued, Kofi's worldview began to warp. He became convinced that the world was a treacherous place, full of predators waiting for the perfect moment to strike. Every news story about violence or harassment felt like confirmation of his worst fears - I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. His friends and family would try to reassure him, but Kofi just couldn't shake the feeling that he was walking on thin ice. One particular incident still haunted him - a night when she'd shown up outside his apartment building, pounding on the door until he'd called the police. The officers had taken her away, but not before she'd spat at him through the window, "You think you can hide from me?" Kofi's mind would replay that moment over and over, convinced that if only he'd done something differently - been more polite to her initially, or blocked her number sooner - none of this would have happened. The event had become a personal failing in his eyes. As the months dragged on, Kofi found himself withdrawing from social events, avoiding coffee shops and public spaces where she might find him. His work began to suffer too - he'd get so caught up in checking his surroundings that he couldn't focus on design tasks. Coworkers noticed his distraction and asked if everything was okay, but Kofi just shrugged it off as stress. The isolation took its toll on Kofi's relationships - friends stopped inviting him out when he kept declining, assuming he was flaking or not interested. His parents worried that something was wrong, but Kofi couldn't bear to tell them about the stalking, convinced they'd be disappointed in his inability to handle it himself. Lately, though, things had reached a breaking point. A new design project required him to collaborate with a team remotely - which meant opening up his laptop camera and screen-sharing for hours on end. Every time he saw his own face staring back at him, Kofi felt like he was inviting another predator into his life. His heart would start racing as he frantically scanned the room behind him, convinced someone was lurking just out of sight. That's when Kofi knew he needed help - not just to deal with the stalking itself, but with the toxic fears and self-blame that had taken hold. He'd finally reached a point where he realized he couldn't shake this alone - what frightened him most was losing himself completely in the darkness of his own mind.
